concept.name: Perpetual futures contract
concept.definition: A futures-style derivative contract, predominant in cryptoasset markets, that has no expiry or settlement date, so a position can be held indefinitely. Its price is kept anchored to an underlying spot index price through periodic funding payments exchanged between long and short position holders.
concept.intuition: A perpetual is a futures contract you never have to roll. A funding fee paid by the more crowded side keeps its price tethered to spot.
concept.mechanics: Positions are leveraged against initial and maintenance margin, marked to a mark price derived from a spot index price, and liquidated if collateral falls below maintenance margin. Funding is paid at fixed intervals (e.g., every 8 hours): when the funding rate is positive, longs pay shorts, and when negative, shorts pay longs; exchanges maintain insurance funds and, as a last resort, auto-deleveraging to absorb bankrupt accounts.
concept.formula: Funding payment = position notional x funding rate; the funding rate is typically composed of an interest rate component plus a premium index measuring the perp's deviation from the spot index price.
concept.failure_modes: Funding rates can become extremely expensive in one-sided markets, turning a correct directional view into a losing carry trade. In extreme volatility, liquidation engines and insurance funds can be overwhelmed, triggering auto-deleveraging that socializes losses onto profitable traders.
concept.misconceptions: That having no expiry means there is no cost of carry — funding is a recurring carry cost that substitutes for the futures roll. Also, the contract price can still deviate from spot under stress; the anchor is an incentive, not a guarantee.
concept.example: A BTCUSDT perpetual trading above its spot index shows a positive funding rate, so every 8 hours long position holders pay shorts a small percentage of their notional, pushing the contract price back toward spot.

citations.source: Binance Academy: What Are Perpetual Futures Contracts?
